https://www.dw.com/en/ferry-carrying-ove.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JdlR Authorities said many of the passengers and crew members were rescued and taken to shore Image: Reuters TV/REUTERS Advertisement A passenger ferry capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, shortly after leaving port, the local government said. At least seven people have died, Turkish state media reported, citing Unal Ustel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) . Ustel said that some 237 people had been rescued, while 23 people were missing. Cyprus has been divided since 1974, with the northern part under the administration of the TRNC, which is recognized internationally only by Turkey . The ferry capsized shortly after departing from the Northern Cyprus port of Kyrenia Image: Reuters TV/REUTERS Passenger boat heading from northern Cyprus to Turkey Turkish media reported that a ferry carrying more than 260 passengers was traveling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, to the Turkish port of Tasucu in southern Mersin province, when it sank. Erhan Arikli, the TRNC's Transport Minister, told Turkish and Cypriot media that there were 267 people on board — 259 passengers and 8 crew members. "All necessary preparations are being made for a swift response from rescue and health services," the TRNC's Health Ministry said in a statement. Search and rescue operations ongoing In a post on X, Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said: "We are closely following the unfortunate incident that has occurred and providing all possible support to the search and rescue efforts." Turkey's state-run TRT news channel reported that the ferry began taking on water 7.5 kilometers (4 nautical miles) from the coast. http://www.bgnes.com/politics/romania-s-.text: Romania is investing millions of euros in Orthodox churches across Moldova, extending its religious and cultural influence into areas traditionally dominated by the Russian Orthodox Church—including the Bulgarian-majority district of Taraclia. In the centre of Aluatu, a village in Taraclia, a new Romanian Orthodox church is being built beside the town hall and school. It is the only parish affiliated with the Romanian Orthodox Church’s Metropolis of Bessarabia among the district’s 25 settlements, where ethnic Bulgarians account for about two-thirds of the population. Bucharest provided approximately €100,000 for the church’s construction last year and allocated another €50,000 for furnishings this summer. Aluatu is unusual within Taraclia because Romanian speakers form the local majority. Although the village officially has 780 residents, only about 500 are believed to live there permanently. Romania has sharply increased its support for church construction and renovation in Moldova since 2024. Under a law adopted in 2023, the government may allocate up to €2 million annually for such projects through the Romanian Patriarchate. Around €4.5 million has been transferred over the past two and a half years, financing 16 churches and nine additional projects involving social centres and monastic facilities, according to Romania’s State Secretariat for Religious Affairs, cited by Radio Free Europe Moldova. The initiative is part of a broader struggle for religious influence between the Metropolis of Bessarabia, which is subordinate to the Romanian Patriarchate, and the Metropolis of Chișinău and All Moldova, which remains under the Moscow Patriarchate. Russia’s war against Ukraine and Patriarch Kirill’s support for it have prompted some Moldovan parishes to leave the Moscow-linked church and join the Romanian jurisdiction. Religious diplomacy researcher Tatiana Cojocari estimates that the share of churches identifying with the Metropolis of Bessarabia has risen from about 12% in 2010 to between 20% and 25% today. Romanian theologian Paul Palencsar described Bucharest’s policy as a form of “soft power”—a message to Romanian-speaking communities beyond the Prut River that they have not been forgotten. Romania has also significantly increased financial support for clergy serving under the Metropolis of Bessarabia. Its monthly payroll for priests in Moldova now exceeds €100,000, approximately ten times the 2018 level. The policy is particularly significant in Taraclia, where about 85% of voters rejected Moldova’s proposed constitutional commitment to European Union membership in the October 2024 referendum. Only the autonomous region of Gagauzia recorded stronger opposition. The new church in Aluatu follows a decades-long dispute over the village’s small Orthodox chapel. It was established by the Metropolis of Bessarabia in 1992 but later passed under the control of the Moscow-linked Moldovan church. Similar Romanian-funded projects are under way in Sângerei, Bălți, Cahul and Ungheni. Supporters describe them as investments in the spiritual and cultural future of Romanian communities between the Prut and Dniester rivers. Analysts warn, however, that buildings and salaries alone will not secure public trust. The Metropolis of Bessarabia must also demonstrate institutional integrity, avoid political interference and distinguish itself clearly from its Moscow-linked rival. Russia, meanwhile, is unlikely to surrender its religious influence in Moldova. Even if wartime pressures limit direct funding, experts expect Moscow to continue using political pressure, clerical networks and other forms of hybrid influence. Construction of the Aluatu church is expected to take at least another two years. Once completed, it will be the first Romanian Orthodox church built in that part of Moldova in roughly a century. | BGNES

https://www.spiked-online.com/2026/09/25.text: Orwell taught us to beware the technocrats Soulless utilitarians are just as deluded and dangerous as naive idealists. i Picture by: Getty Patrick West Columnist 25th September 2026 i Picture by: Getty Share Topics Politics UK Want unlimited, ad-free access? Become a spiked supporter . Whenever the patrician concerns, fringe obsessions or neurotic fixations of lifestyle leftists make the news, it invariably brings to mind George Orwell’s withering observations of a similar demographic he identified in the 1930s. So when it emerged last week that the Department of Education had issued new food guidance banning fish and chips, fried eggs and pastries from schools , and recommending in their stead dishes with lentils and other pulses, I won’t have been alone in recalling the repeated complaints he made in The Road to Wigan Pier (1937) about a type of ‘fruit-juice drinker, nudist, sandal-wearer, sex-maniac, Quaker, “Nature Cure” quack, pacifist and feminist’ then found on the British left. This variety of upper-middle-class leftist still lives on. You’ll find him – or, more likely, her – looking for the ethically sourced, environmentally friendly vegan foods in Waitrose, flying the Progress Pride Flag or wearing a keffiyeh, repeating platitudes about ‘equity and inclusion’ or publicly atoning for their ‘white privilege’. Yet it’s sometimes forgotten that Orwell discerned a second species of refined socialist, whose aloof idealism was also removed from the everyday concerns of ordinary people. These were the materialist, technocratic, future-orientated visionaries like HG Wells and Aldous Huxley, who thought that a new world could be created in the Soviet Union. Even worse were the likes of Beatrice Webb and Labour intellectual Harold Laski, who believed that a socialist utopia was already being established in the USSR. This was an upper echelon, Orwell wrote, who reeked of ‘crankishness, machine-worship and the stupid cult of Russia’. Their socialism evoked in the minds of the common man ‘a picture of aeroplanes, tractors and huge glittering factories of glass’ – to use a description Huxley gave in his most famous book, Brave New World . For Orwell, it was a vision advanced by a ‘large army of scientists and technicians… marching along the road of “progress” with the blind persistence of a column of ants’. That kind of inhuman, utilitarian, leftist and – in modern parlance – centrist also survives today. They were the Blairite neophiliacs who deprecated ‘the past’. They’re the GDP-fetishists who told us in the 2016 Brexit referendum that ‘the economy’ was more important than the nation, democracy and self-determination. They’re the pedantic and robotic lawyers who believe obedience to international treaties overrides the concerns of British people. They’re the ones, like education secretary Lucy Powell , who want to remove the classical and humanistic elements from the school curriculum in the pursuit of ‘skills’. They believe that public bodies have a socioeconomic duty to implement equality in the workplace. They’re the DEI-obsessed bureaucrats forever calculating the racial composition of public-sector bodies. They favour immigration because they think people are identical, replaceable units. They resort to graphs and statistics to prove a point. These are the Net Zero ideologues who focus on an abstract future while ignoring the needs of the present. They treat society as a machine to be corrected, fixed and made perfect. Orwell never found this type of deluded socialist remotely amusing, and neither should we. Cate Blanchett is right – put your phone away It’s heartening to see more famous people recommending that we liberate ourselves from smartphones. Last Friday, Cate Blanchett became the latest theatre star to ask her audience to stop filming during performances. Her fellow thespian, the globe-trotter Michael Palin, has also suggested that tourists should learn to savour the moment. As he told the Telegraph on Saturday : Recommended Gaza: the most lied about war in history Brendan O'Neill 'The problem is everybody gets to a wonderful place where all the cameras go out. So you’ve immediately got a screen between you and what you’re seeing. Just use your eyes and ears. Take it in yourself.' I confess that I’m no better than most, having taken the opportunity of a day trip to Bruges on Sunday to photograph the Belgian town’s beautiful and historic buildings – and then put the results online. But I also like taking photos of tourists taking photos. I couldn’t help doing so in London last week as I passed through Westminster Square, having spotted a long line of people waiting to have their picture taken next to a classic, decommissioned red telephone kiosk facing Big Ben. Just as wokery isn’t dead, this indicates that we also still live in a postmodern society – even though postmodernism was similarly pronounced finished decades ago. Here were people queuing in front of an object that no longer had a function and only served now as an unmoored signifier (of ‘historic Britishness’), to synthesise an event, rather than experience it, in order to place a representation of it in a hyperreal realm to prove that they existed in the corporeal one. Podcast Why I quit the Democrats spiked The French sociologist Jean Baudrillard, who sadly never lived to see the dawn of social media, would have been fascinated by this performative simulation of actual living. He might even have been interested in my photo of these tourists taking photos, which I also put up online. Very ‘meta’, as they say these days. The myth of ‘Brexit travel chaos’ Ever since Britain officially left the EU in 2020, there has been a certain type of tedious Remainer who forever posts pictures of being stuck in queues at continental airports, whining about the indignity of being a second-class, non-EU citizen. In their minds, a single lived experience seems to constitute a coherent argument. Unfortunately, it also implies that they believe that convenience is more important than democracy or sovereignty. When I passed through passport control at Dover Port on Sunday, on my first visit to the continent since we left the EU, I had no such trouble. We all waited in line for 10 minutes. The French official at the desk didn’t look inside my passport or even look me in the eye. I might as well have said, Alan Partridge-style: ‘ Hello, I’m a Communist with a gun .’ While there were two tiers of passport control at Dunkirk on the return leg, getting through it took even less time than it used to. The French official didn’t ask me to remove my spectacles – as was mandatory pre-Brexit – and he even smiled! The British official addressed me by my first name as we parted. I know I’m not alone. One friend remarks that while he has faced delays entering Poland and at Amsterdam’s Schiphol airport, there were none in Rotterdam. He has made his way seamlessly through the eGates at Barcelona Airport. Another regular visitor to Italy also reports no holdups. So much for the ‘nightmare’ of travelling to the EU. In my ‘lived experience’, the only thing that has changed tangibly, and for the better, is the return of duty-free shopping.
